notes: BANK RECONCILIATION: WHAT IT OFFERS YOU, WHAT IT CHECKS, AND WHAT IT KEEPS. THREE THINGS YOU ASKED FOR. Reversing a stale cheque now asks for the date instead of stamping today, and refuses one before the cheque was written, in the future, in a closed period, or inside a month already signed off. A receipt posted from the reconciliation screen is no longer limited to revenue: a debtor settling an invoice or a student paying outstanding fees can go to the right account, and the rule is enforced when you save, not only in the list you pick from. And when a line has exactly one candidate at the same amount, Match ticks it and scrolls to it rather than making you read down a long list for an answer it already had. MATCH CAN FIND A CHEQUE THE BANK NAMED BUT DID NOT TOTAL. A line reading INWARD CLEARING CHEQUE 969880 for 3,515.62 is two cheques, 3,373.62 and 142.00. Neither carries the line's figure, so neither was ever offered, while the line names one of them in plain sight. Match now also reads the words the bank printed: an item is offered when the line names its reference, and when it is a suffix sibling of one it names, 969880-C beside 969880. That is not a nicety. When a cheque book number is written twice the register extends it, thirteen numbers on one real account do exactly that, and the bank prints only the base number. Already cleared rows can be ticked and re-dated as a set, and re-dating checks EVERY month those items clear in today, not only the month they are moving to. RECONCILING ITEMS THAT WERE NEVER YOURS. Left the bank with no cheque was counting a cheque's own reversal, a lodgement closed against a journal, and a withholding remittance paid by a cheque the register already holds. One cheque settles more than one voucher, and the extra vouchers were being counted as money that left the bank on its own: on one real account, eighteen phantom rows worth 10,263.11, a difference that could never be explained because nothing was actually wrong. EACH SCHEDULE ADDS UP TO ITS OWN TOTAL. A schedule could print a total its own rows did not add to. Each now foots its own rows, and Schedules 3 and 4 are printed and exported too, so every figure in the summary has a schedule behind it. THE REGISTER AND THE LEDGER, CHECKED AGAINST EACH OTHER. Before you sign off, the screen asks whether each cheque's registered amount is what the bank actually moved on the vouchers it settles. A cheque registered at the wrong figure moves the unpresented total, so a month can tie for the wrong reason. A warning, never a refusal, and shown whether or not the month ties. THE DIFFERENCE EXPLAINS ITSELF, AND SOONER. The cheap questions are asked first, a blank statement balance is now the only answer given rather than a list of subtler causes, the balance is filled in from an imported statement that actually covers your date, and the schedules say how far back your statements reach. A SIGNED OFF MONTH IS PROTECTED BY THE LEDGER ITSELF. The rule that a filed month cannot be re-stated behind your back is now enforced by the database, so it holds whichever screen, import or action is involved. It is precise: presenting a January cheque in February is not a change to January and is not refused. A FILED RECONCILIATION IS KEPT, NOT REPLACED. Signing again used to overwrite what was signed before. Every signed version is now kept, its figures and the schedule rows behind them, listed newest first. Nothing can edit or delete one, including the app itself. A CHEQUE NUMBER CAN BE CORRECTED. An administrator can correct a number written in wrong, with a reason and an audit record. A number already used on that account is refused. INSTALLING: this version adds tables and checks to your ledger, so it is not a pure code update. It installs straight over the previous version and your data is migrated in place, but please take a backup first: Backup and Export, Back up now.
